final_proof:
The claim as stated is false. Indeed, it already fails in the Banach space V = R. Let N = {0,1,2,...}, take I = J = K = N, and define v_0 = r and v_i = 0 for every i > 0. Enumerate J by j_n = n, and enumerate K by k_0 = 1, k_1 = 0, and k_n = n for n >= 2. These are both bijective enumerations of N. Then

∑_{n=1}^∞ v_{j_n} = 0,

so the first series is absolutely convergent but has sum 0, not r (recall that r > 0). On the other hand,

∑_{n=1}^∞ v_{k_n} = v_{k_1} + ∑_{n=2}^∞ v_{k_n} = v_0 + 0 = r,

and this series is absolutely convergent. Thus the right-hand assertion is true and the left-hand assertion is false. The defect is that the enumerations begin with j_0 and k_0, whereas the displayed series omit those terms. There is also a typing issue in the general formulation: for an arbitrary Banach space V, a positive real number r need not be an element of V.

A natural corrected statement is the following. Let x be an element of V. Under the other stated hypotheses,

∑_{n=0}^∞ v_{j_n} converges absolutely to x if and only if ∑_{n=0}^∞ v_{k_n} converges absolutely to x.

(When V = R, one may take x = r.) We now prove this corrected statement.

Assume that ∑_{n=0}^∞ v_{j_n} converges absolutely to x. Put a_n = v_{j_n}, b_m = v_{k_m}, p_N = ∑_{n=0}^N a_n, and q_M = ∑_{m=0}^M b_m. Absolute convergence gives

L := ∑_{n=0}^∞ ||a_n|| < ∞,

and p_N tends to x.

First we show that the b-series is absolutely convergent. Fix M. Whenever 0 <= m <= M and b_m != 0, the index k_m belongs to the nonzero support of the family. By hypothesis that support is contained in J ∩ K, so k_m belongs to J. Since (j_n) is a bijective enumeration of J, there is a unique n(m) such that j_{n(m)} = k_m. Distinct m give distinct n(m), and b_m = a_{n(m)}. Consequently,

∑_{m=0}^M ||b_m|| = ∑_{0 <= m <= M, b_m != 0} ||a_{n(m)}|| <= ∑_{n=0}^∞ ||a_n|| = L.

The partial sums of the nonnegative real series ∑ ||b_m|| are therefore increasing and bounded above, so ∑_{m=0}^∞ ||b_m|| converges.

It remains to identify the vector sum. Let ε > 0. Choose N sufficiently large that

||p_N - x|| < ε/2 and ∑_{n>N} ||a_n|| < ε/2.

Among a_0,...,a_N there are only finitely many nonzero terms. If a_n != 0 for some n <= N, then j_n lies in the nonzero support and hence in K; therefore it occurs as k_m for a unique m. Choose M_0 so large that k_0,...,k_{M_0} include the indices of every nonzero term among a_0,...,a_N. For any M >= M_0, all those terms occur in q_M. Every other nonzero term occurring in q_M equals a_n for a unique n > N. Hence, for some finite set E_M contained in {n : n > N},

q_M - p_N = ∑_{n in E_M} a_n.

By the triangle inequality,

||q_M - p_N|| <= ∑_{n in E_M} ||a_n|| <= ∑_{n>N} ||a_n|| < ε/2.

It follows that

||q_M - x|| <= ||q_M - p_N|| + ||p_N - x|| < ε

for every M >= M_0. Thus q_M tends to x. Together with convergence of ∑ ||b_m||, this says that ∑_{m=0}^∞ v_{k_m} converges absolutely to x.

The same argument with J and K interchanged proves the converse. This establishes the corrected equivalence.
